interviewQuestions.question: How would you find the length of the longest increasing subsequence in an array?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd define `dp[i]` as the length of the longest increasing chain that ends exactly at index `i` — not the best chain among the first `i` elements, specifically one that terminates there. That precision matters because it's what lets the recurrence work.

For each `i`, I look at every earlier index `j`. If `nums[j] < nums[i]`, I could extend that chain by appending `nums[i]`, giving length `dp[j] + 1`. So `dp[i] = max(dp[j] + 1)` over all valid `j`, or 1 if nothing smaller came before it — the chain of just itself.

The final answer is `max(dp)` across every index, since the longest chain overall might end anywhere, not necessarily at the last element. This is O(n²): for each of n elements, I scan up to n earlier ones. I'd mention up front that there's a faster O(n log n) approach using a different state representation, and offer to walk through it if useful — proactively flagging that trade-off tends to read well.

**Testing:** whether you can derive the O(n²) recurrence cleanly and articulate what dp[i] actually represents, which is where most candidates get imprecise.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Can you improve LIS to O(n log n)? Walk me through the idea.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Yes — the trick is to stop tracking 'the best chain ending at each position' and instead track 'the smallest tail value achievable for each chain length,' in an array I usually call `tails`.

The key insight: if two chains have the same length but different tail values, the one with the smaller tail is always at least as useful going forward — anything that could extend the larger-tailed chain can also extend the smaller-tailed one. So I only ever need to remember the best (smallest) tail per length, discarding everything else as dominated.

Processing each new number, I binary-search `tails` for the leftmost position whose value is >= the current number. If I find one, I overwrite it — this number gives a smaller-or-equal tail for that same chain length. If I don't find one, the number extends the longest chain seen so far, so I append it, growing `tails` by one. Because `tails` stays sorted throughout, this search is O(log n), giving O(n log n) total.

The answer is simply the final length of `tails`. One caveat I'd flag unprompted: `tails` itself is not a valid subsequence of the original array by the end — its length is correct, but its contents aren't reconstructable as-is.

**Testing:** whether you actually understand the domination argument behind patience sorting, or have just memorized the binary-search code.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Optimization

interviewQuestions.question: The interviewer now asks for the actual longest increasing subsequence, not just its length. Does your O(n log n) approach still work?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Not directly, and I'd say so rather than trying to force it. The `tails` array in the patience-sorting approach only ever holds the smallest tail per chain length — its entries get overwritten by unrelated later values, so reading it as a sequence at the end generally doesn't correspond to any subsequence that actually existed together in the input.

To recover the real subsequence with the fast approach, I'd need to augment it: alongside overwriting `tails[pos]`, also record, for the element just placed, which element it logically followed — the current last element of `tails[pos - 1]` at that moment. That gives a set of 'predecessor' links I can walk backward from the end of the final `tails` array to reconstruct one valid LIS, still in O(n log n) overall since it's O(1) extra bookkeeping per element.

Alternatively, and more simply if reconstruction was the ask from the start, I'd fall back to the O(n²) DP with an explicit `prev[i]` array recording which earlier index each `dp[i]` extended from — that reconstruction is more direct to explain and implement correctly under time pressure, at the cost of the slower complexity.

I'd make the trade-off explicit to the interviewer rather than silently picking one: faster algorithm with more bookkeeping, or slower algorithm with a simpler reconstruction.

**Testing:** whether you recognize that an optimization can trade away information you need for a follow-up ask, and whether you can propose a real fix rather than hand-waving.
